intro: The Danish String Quartet plays a C minor lament in which the first violin seems to improvise above three players singing a hymn. Haydn leaves the ending suspended and sends the music straight into the minuet.

sections.label: A · C minor, violin and chorale
sections.mNote: The first violin decorates the lower three players’ slow melody

sections.label: B · Changing chords beneath the violin
sections.mNote: The violin keeps moving above the held accompaniment

sections.label: C · C minor, then a held G
sections.mNote: Morendo: the music fades towards the minuet

cues.title: A violin above a hymn
cues.text: The second violin, viola and cello sing a slow melody in C minor. Above them the first violin winds through quick, elaborate flourishes, as if the four players have quite different ideas about how much time a phrase needs.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Adagio, pp. 188–190. Laurie Shulman describes the first violin’s rhapsodic line above a chorale in the other three instruments: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three steady companions
cues.text: The lower instruments hold their notes while the first violin runs on. Its little turns and sudden leaps stretch across the chords; the accompaniment keeps its patient pace.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Adagio, pp. 188–189; Shulman’s account of the ornamental violin line and chorale accompaniment. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Tost takes the quartets
cues.text: In late 1788 Johann Tost heads for Paris carrying six new Haydn quartets and two symphonies. Until March he has been the Esterházy orchestra’s principal second violin; now he is doing business with the publisher Sieber.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, programme note for the Schumann Quartet, 20 November 2022, p. 2: Tost’s service, Paris visit and negotiations. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: The unfinished ending
cues.text: The closing passage is marked morendo — dying away. A held G leaves C minor waiting for an answer. Haydn writes attacca: the C major minuet follows without a break.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 190: morendo, final G with fermata and attacca. Shulman confirms the unbroken connection to the Menuetto. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He could empty an orchestra one player at a time, or keep a quartet going after everyone thought the piece had ended.
facts: St Stephen’s choir, Vienna · accompanying Nicola Porpora · studying C. P. E. Bach
The Esterházy princes, from 1761 until his death
104 numbered symphonies · quartets · keyboard music · operas · masses and oratorios

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
